title: 0.10 Reading files
objectives: Open a text file with `with open(path, encoding='utf-8')` and explain why `with` guarantees the file is closed
Loop over a file line by line, strip each line, skip blank lines, and explain why a second loop over the same file gets nothing
Validate every line of a messy GPS log (junk, blank lines, bad checksums, a truncated last line) and count the errors
Explain relative vs absolute paths and the current working directory, and write functions that take the path as a parameter

predict.question: Each sentence written here is 6 characters long. What does the reading loop print?
predict.code:
with open("t.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("$GPGGA\n$GPRMC\n")

with open("t.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(len(line))
predict.why:
Every line you get from a file keeps its newline character, so each line is 6 visible characters plus '
' = 7. The file ends right after the second '
', so there is no third, empty line: the loop runs exactly twice. That invisible '
' is why you always strip() before comparing or slicing from the end.

predict.question: What does this print?
predict.code:
with open("t.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("$GPGGA\n$GPRMC\n$GPGSV\n")

with open("t.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    first = len(f.readlines())
    second = len(f.readlines())
print(first, second)
predict.why: A file object has a read position, like a tape head. The first readlines() reads all 3 lines and leaves the position at the end of the file. The second readlines() starts at the end, finds nothing, and returns an empty list. There is no error, which makes this bug hard to spot. Read once and keep the list, or do all the work in one loop.

predict.question: The read happens after the with-block. What happens?
predict.code:
with open("t.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("$GPGGA\n")

with open("t.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    pass
print(f.read())
predict.why: The with-block closed the file when it ended. The name f still exists, but it now refers to a CLOSED file, and reading a closed file raises ValueError: I/O operation on closed file. The file is still on disk (so it isn't FileNotFoundError); you just have to do your reading inside the with-block.

visualizations.title: Trace: the strip-and-skip loop

props.code:
import io

# io.StringIO behaves like an open text file, but lives in memory.
f = io.StringIO("$GPGGA,,,,,,0,00,,,M,,M,,*66\n\n$GPGGA,153015.00,4220.01")
count = 0
blank = 0
for line in f:
    line = line.strip()
    if line == "":
        blank += 1
        continue
    count += 1
print(count, blank)

visualizations.notice: Watch line in the variables table: on each pass it first holds the raw line WITH '\n', then the stripped copy. The middle line becomes '' and takes the continue path. The last line has no '\n' at all (the file was cut off), and this loop happily counts it, because it only skips blanks and never validates. That's why the challenge also checks the checksum.

predictFirst.question: How many times will the loop body run? What will line hold on the first pass before and after strip()? What gets printed at the end?
predictFirst.reveal: 3 passes, one per line. First pass: '$GPGGA,,,,,,0,00,,,M,,M,,*66\n', then the same without the '\n'. The blank line adds 1 to blank. It prints 2 1: the truncated line is counted as a sentence because nothing checks it.

challenge.task: Write load_sentences(path) that opens a GPS log with `with open(path, encoding='utf-8')`, returns (sentences, errors): the stripped, checksum-valid NMEA sentences in file order, and the count of non-blank lines rejected (junk, bad checksum, truncated). Blank lines are skipped and are not errors. The checksum rule is shown in the NMEA checksum table next to the challenge.

explainBack.prompt: In your own words: walk through how your load_sentences reads a log file. Why do you use `with`, why must every line be stripped, how does your code tell a blank line from a bad one, and why does a truncated last line end up counted as an error? Finally, why is the path a parameter instead of a file name written inside the function?
rubric: Explains that `with` closes the file automatically when the block ends (even on an error), and that each line from the loop keeps its '\n' so it must be stripped (and the result stored)
Explains that a stripped blank line is '' and is skipped with continue, while junk, corrupted, and truncated lines fail the checksum check (no '$', no '*', or a mismatched checksum) and are counted
Explains that relative paths depend on the current working directory, so taking the path as a parameter lets the caller (or the tests) point the function at any file

challenge: Start from the standard log-reading loop in the lesson. What does a blank line look like after strip()? And which single check rejects a boot banner, a corrupted sentence, AND a truncated line?

Make an empty list and an error counter. Open the file with `with` and encoding='utf-8', loop over it, strip each line, and `continue` on ''. If the checksum is valid, append the stripped line; otherwise add 1 to the errors. After the with-block, return both as a tuple. For checksum_ok: find the '*', check the line starts with '$' and a '*' exists, XOR every character between them, and compare that (as 2 uppercase hex digits) with the text after the '*' uppercased.

load_sentences(path): sentences = empty list; errors = 0. With the file at path open for reading (utf-8) as f: for each line in f: line = stripped line; if line is empty: skip to the next line; if checksum_ok(line): add line to sentences; else: errors = errors + 1. Return (sentences, errors). checksum_ok(s): star = position of '*' in s; if s doesn't start with '$' or star is -1: return False; x = 0; for each character between index 1 and star: x = x XOR its code; return (x as 2-digit uppercase hex) == (s after star, uppercased).
bug: Put a print(line) inside the second loop and run it. How many times does it print? Where is the file's read position after the first loop finishes?

The first loop reads the file to the end, so the second loop over the same file object gets no lines at all. Count both things in ONE loop (or save the lines in a list first and loop over the list twice).
